text: Your loop just read z[i]. Spatial locality says the next read is probably a {{c1::nearby}} address, like z[i+1]. Temporal locality says you will read the {{c2::same}} address again soon.
extra: The cache loads a whole block around each miss, so both habits turn into cache hits.

text: Walk a plain array and each element sits right after the last one in memory, so you get spatial locality for {{c1::free}}. Walk a linked list and the next node can be {{c2::far away}} in memory.
extra: That is why parallel code goes back to contiguous arrays instead of linked data.

text: Lecture 7's quick rules for cache-friendly data are structs instead of objects, {{c1::no pointers}} inside structs, and {{c2::contiguous arrays}} instead of linked data.
extra: A pointer sends the CPU to some other address, and that breaks spatial locality.

text: Contiguous data is easy to transfer because you just move {{c1::N bytes starting at address M}}. That is how one big array goes out as a single MPI message or a single copy to the GPU.
extra: MPI programs and CPU plus GPU programs move large blocks all the time, so the layout decides how much transfer overhead you pay.

text: In parallel code a 2D array is really a {{c1::1D}} array with index math. With \(n\) columns, row \(i\) and column \(j\) sit at position {{c2::\(i \cdot n + j\)}}.
extra: Rows are stored one after another, so the whole grid stays one contiguous block.

text: Your old single-core computer is {{c1::SISD}}. It runs one instruction on one piece of data at a time, which is the classic von Neumann machine.
extra: Flynn's taxonomy counts instruction streams and data streams. The four types are SISD, SIMD, MISD, and MIMD.

text: Picture one control unit driving several ALUs, each running the same instruction on its own data. That is {{c1::SIMD}}, and with \(m\) ALUs the arithmetic runs up to {{c2::\(m\)}} times faster.
extra: Classic SIMD suits simple loops over big arrays. It helps with data parallelism and not much else.

text: Several instruction streams working on one data stream is {{c1::MISD}}. Hardly any real systems work this way.
extra: It mostly exists to complete the four boxes of the taxonomy.

text: {{c1::MIMD}} is the general-purpose parallel machine. Each core has its own ALU and runs {{c2::asynchronously}}, at its own pace.
extra: A MIMD machine can be shared memory or distributed memory. Your multicore laptop and an MPI cluster are both MIMD.

text: A vector processor is a kind of SIMD machine. It loads arrays into {{c1::vector registers}} and applies the {{c2::same}} operation to every element at once.
extra: Vector length is fixed per system, usually between 4 and 256 elements of 64 bits each.

text: Vector processors are fast and easy to use because compilers are good at {{c1::vectorizing}} loops. They also have high memory bandwidth, and {{c2::all}} the data they load gets used.
extra: A cache line can bring in words your code never touches. A vector load brings in only the elements the operation uses.

text: Vector processors struggle with {{c1::irregular}} data structures, meaning anything that is not an array. They are also hard to scale, because {{c2::longer}} vectors do not help much.
extra: These are the two drawbacks on the Lecture 14 slide.

text: In shared-memory MIMD, cores communicate {{c1::implicitly}} by reading and writing shared data. In distributed-memory MIMD, each core has private memory and communicates {{c2::explicitly}} by sending messages.
extra: Pthreads is the shared-memory model. MPI is the distributed-memory model.

text: In a {{c1::UMA}} system, every core reaches every memory location in the same time. That makes it {{c2::easier to program}}, because you never worry about where the data lives.
extra: UMA stands for uniform memory access. The memory is one big chunk on a shared bus.

text: In a {{c1::NUMA}} system, each chip has its own block of memory. A core reads its own chip's memory {{c2::faster}} than another chip's. In exchange you get room for {{c3::more memory}} than UMA.
extra: NUMA stands for nonuniform memory access. Access time depends on which chip owns the address.

text: A cluster is a set of ordinary computers joined by a commodity network like {{c1::Ethernet}}. Each node is usually a shared-memory machine itself, so people call it a {{c2::hybrid}} system.
extra: A grid spreads several clusters over a large area. Its nodes are often heterogeneous, meaning they run different hardware and operating systems.

text: A {{c1::bus}} is the cheap, flexible way to connect cores and memory, but every device shares the same wires. Add more processors and they spend more time {{c2::waiting}} for memory.
extra: This contention is why large shared-memory systems moved to switched interconnects.

text: A crossbar switch gives each CPU its own path to a memory module, so it is {{c1::faster}} than a bus. Two CPUs only conflict when they use the {{c2::same}} memory module. The catch is that crossbars are {{c3::expensive}}.
extra: With four CPUs and four memory modules, all four CPUs can read or write at the same time without blocking each other.
